etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English water, from Old English wæter (“water”), from Proto-West Germanic *watar, from Proto-Germanic *watōr (“water”), from Proto-Indo-European *wódr̥ (“water”).

definitions.definition: (uncountable, in particular) The liquid form of this substance: liquid H2O.

quote.citation: 1835, Sir John Ross, Sir James Clark Ross, Narrative of a Second Voyage in Search of a North-west Passage …, Volume 1, pages 284–5:
quote.text: Towards the following morning, the thermometer fell to 5°; and at daylight, there was not an atom of water to be seen in any direction.

quote.citation: 2002, Arthur T. Hubbard, Encyclopedia of Surface and Colloid Science, →ISBN, page 4895:
quote.text: A water drop placed on the surface of ice can either spread or form a lens depending on the properties of the three phases involved in wetting, i.e., on the properties of the ice, water, and gas phases.

quote.citation: 2013 May 11, “The climate of Tibet: Pole-land”, in The Economist, volume 407, number 8835, page 80:
quote.text: Of all the transitions brought about on the Earth’s surface by temperature change, the melting of ice into water is the starkest. It is binary. And for the land beneath, the air above and the life around, it changes everything.

definitions.definition: (countable) A serving of liquid water.

quote.citation: 2006, Lori Foster, Erin McCarthy, Amy Garvey, Bad Boys of Summer, →ISBN, page 91:
quote.text: Joe bustled back and offered her a glass of wine but she shook her head. “Just a water, please.”

definitions.definition: (uncountable) A substance (of molecular formula H2O) found at room temperature and pressure as a clear liquid; it is present naturally as rain, and found in rivers, lakes and seas; its solid form is ice and its gaseous form is steam.

quote.citation: 1805 December, Julius Griffiths, “A Journey across the Desert”, in The Monthly Mirror, page 362:
quote.text: It is wholly out of the power of language to convey any idea of the blissful enjoyment of obtaining water, after an almost total want of it, during eight and forty hours, in the scorching regions of an Arabian desert, in the month of July.

quote.citation: 2013 September-October, Katie L. Burke, “In the News”, in American Scientist:
quote.text: Oxygen levels on Earth skyrocketed 2.4 billion years ago, when cyanobacteria evolved photosynthesis: the ability to convert water and carbon dioxide into carbohydrates and waste oxygen using solar energy.

definitions.definition: (alchemy, philosophy) The aforementioned liquid, considered one of the Classical elements or basic elements of alchemy.
(uncountable or in the plural) Water in a body; an area of open water.

quote.citation: c. 1595–1596 (date written), William Shakespeare, “Loues Labour’s Lost”, in Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies […] (First Folio), London:  […]  Isaac Iaggard, and Ed[ward] Blount, published 1623, →OCLC, [Act V, scene i], page 138, column 2:
quote.text: Roſa. O vain peticioner, beg a greater matter,Thou now requeſts but Mooneſhine in the water.

quote.citation: 1913, Joseph C[rosby] Lincoln, chapter I, in Mr. Pratt’s Patients, New York, N.Y., London: D[aniel] Appleton and Company, →OCLC:
quote.text: 'Twas early June, the new grass was flourishing everywheres, the posies in the yard—peonies and such—in full bloom, the sun was shining, and the water of the bay was blue, with light green streaks where the shoal showed.

quote.text:
The president expressed hope that creating rain over waters between the countries would help reduce pollution.

definitions.definition: (poetic, archaic or dialectal) A body of water, almost always a river, sometimes a lake or reservoir, especially in the names given to such bodies.

quote.citation: 1526, [William Tyndale, transl.], The Newe Testamẽt […] (Tyndale Bible), [Worms, Germany: Peter Schöffer], →OCLC, Acts viij:[36], folio clxvi, recto:
quote.text: And as they went on their waye  they cam vnto a certayne water  and the gelded man ſayde: Se here is water  what ſhall lett me to be baptiſed?

quote.citation: 1842, Alfred Tennyson, “Morte d’Arthur”, in Poems. […], volume II, London: Edward Moxon, […], →OCLC, page 4:
quote.text: On one side lay the Ocean, and on oneLay a great water, and the moon was full.

quote.citation: 1865, William Allingham, editor, The Ballad Book: a selection of the choicest British ballads, William and May Margaret, or the Water of Clyde:
quote.text: But ere he came to Clyde's water, fu' loud the wind did blaw.

definitions.definition: (sometimes countable) Mineral water.
(countable, often in the plural) Spa water.
(pharmacy) A solution in water of a gaseous or readily volatile substance.
Urine. [from 15th c.]

quote.citation: 1999, George R.R. Martin, A Clash of Kings, Bantam, published 2011, page 458:
quote.text: Ser Dunaver's squire Jodge could not hold his water when he slept.

definitions.definition: Amniotic fluid or the amniotic sac containing it. (Used only in the plural in the UK but often also in the singular in North America.)
(colloquial, medicine) Fluids in the body, especially when causing swelling.
A combination of water and other substance(s).
(business, often attributive) The water supply, as a service or utility.
(figuratively, in the plural or in the singular) A state of affairs; conditions; usually with an adjective indicating an adverse condition.
(colloquial, figuratively) A person's intuition.
(uncountable, dated, finance) Excess valuation of securities.

quote.citation: 1902 August 2, “Too Much Water to Suit Cummins”, in The Atlanta Constitution:
quote.text: Iowa Governor Will Fight Rock Island Reorganization. He Says That Under the New Plan Too Much Water Is Put Into the Stock—Believes Plan Is Out of Harmony with Iowa Laws.

quote.text: the outstanding stock and bond obligations of the company were reduced from $34,000,000 to $24,000,000 by squeezing out the water.

definitions.definition: The limpidity and lustre of a precious stone, especially a diamond.

quote.citation: 1928, Virginia Woolf, Orlando: A Biography, London: The Hogarth Press, →OCLC; republished as Orlando: A Biography (eBook no. 0200331h.html), Australia: Project Gutenberg Australia, July 2015:
quote.text: And when she raised it to see what caused this agitation, she saw nothing—nothing but the vast solitary emerald which Queen Elizabeth had given her. And was that not enough? she asked. It was of the finest water.

definitions.definition: A wavy, lustrous pattern or decoration such as is imparted to linen, silk, metals, etc.
A particular quality or appearance suggestive of water:

etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English wateren, from Old English wæterian, from Proto-Germanic *watrōną, *watrijaną, from Proto-Germanic *watōr (“water”), from Proto-Indo-European *wódr̥ (“water”).

definitions.definition: (transitive) To pour water into the soil surrounding (plants).

quote.citation: 1900, L. Frank Baum, chapter 24, in The Wonderful Wizard of Oz:
quote.text: Aunt Em had just come out of the house to water the cabbages when she looked up and saw Dorothy running toward her.

definitions.definition: (transitive) To wet or supply with water; to moisten; to overflow with water; to irrigate.

quote.citation: 2008, Oisin Curran, Mopus, page 34:
quote.text: While they watered and washed their horses, I talked with a red-capped man, some kind of chief.

definitions.definition: (intransitive) To get or take in water.

quote.text: After working the 1.30 p.m. through train from Forres to Aberdeen as far as Elgin, she returns tender first with a local passenger train and is then coaled and watered at Forres shed, and eventually works back to Perth on the 10.20 p.m. through freight.

definitions.definition: (intransitive) To fill with or secrete water or similar liquid.
(transitive) To wet and calender, as cloth, so as to impart to it a lustrous appearance in wavy lines; to diversify with wavelike lines.
